articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday pulled up Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut over his remarks targeting Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and the judiciary. The court observed that apologies should come from the heart and not the mind.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi was hearing the contempt case filed by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA). Raut appeared physically before the court, while Waghle joined the proceedings virtually, in compliance with the court's earlier directions.During the hearing, SCBA president and senior advocate Pradeep Rai told the bench that although Raut had apologised for his comments, he had subsequently made social media posts against the Supreme Court. Rai also pointed out that Raut had shared a photograph of the Supreme Court of Albania being set on fire by protesters.Justice Kumar reminded Raut of the responsibility that came with his experience as a politician and parliamentarian."Mr. Sanjay Raut, you are a seasoned politician, we have been hearing your speeches from advocate days. You are a seasoned parliamentarian, and you yourself were in the press. You should know what should be the restraint," he said, as reported by LiveLaw.The Supreme Court had issued show-cause notices to Raut and Waghle on October 16 over their alleged remarks against the CJI and the judiciary.The contempt proceedings stem from the controversy surrounding CJI Surya Kant's decision to decline a request for a personal meeting by a delegation of opposition leaders, asking them instead to approach the court through a petition.According to the SCBA's petition, Waghle had posted an alleged abusive remark against the CJI on X in response to a report about the decision, before deleting it and issuing an apology.Raut, meanwhile, had allegedly questioned the conduct of judges, claiming that some had attended political programmes organised by the BJP and participated in dinners hosted by chief ministers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Nvidia in crisis, AI boom at a crossroads: The tech industry's trillion-dollar bet put to the test
articles.summary: Leather jacket is gone Jensen Huang was the face of Nvidia for decades, as he turned the company into one of the most valuable in the world.
articles.body: Leather jacket is goneJensen Huang was the face of Nvidia for decades, as he turned the company into one of the most valuable in the world. Huang (wearing his black leather jacket) was one of those CEOs whose face and company became synonymous with the AI industry.For long it was the world’s most valuable company, closing competing with Apple. Now, Huang's exit as CEO, announced on November 12 has raised questions about corporate leadership, national security and the company's position at the centre of the global AI race. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, in a letter shared publicly. There are also reports about his alleged ties with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing, a claim China has repeatedly denied.This comes in a time when the entire industry is already quite volatile. The tech giants have been investing billions into advanced chips, data centers, and computing power on the assumption that AI could change businesses and create new revenue models.Nvidia cannot be ignored here. This is because it provides the processors needed to create and operate these state-of-the-art AI models. It thus links the semiconductor makers, cloud computing providers, data center firms, and artificial intelligence developers.The key question is whether the Nvidia crisis will remain limited to the company or shake confidence in the wider AI industry. Could it trigger a broader reassessment of an industry whose valuations and investments increasingly depend on a handful of tech giants?Why one company matters so muchNvidia designs graphics processing units (GPUs), specialised chips capable of performing thousands of calculations simultaneously. This makes them particularly useful for AI systems, which need massive computing power to process data, learn patterns and generate responses.Additionally, Nvidia with its software platform, developer tools and specialised libraries have created an ecosystem around its chips. Companies have spent years building applications and infrastructure optimised for this specific firm, making it difficult to switch suppliers.As for Nvidia’s financial standing, its market capitalisation crossed $5.5 trillion in October. However, by November 12, its valuation had fallen below $4 trillion, shedding a substantial part of its record market value.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The decline was not just due to the latest controversy alone. Investors were already concerned about massive AI infrastructure investments, debt-funded data-centre expansion and whether revenues from AI applications would justify the spending.The pressure was visible across other technology stocks too. On November 5, the Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.52 per cent, while the S&P 500 fell 4.36 per cent. Nvidia lost 9.26 per cent and rival chipmaker AMD dropped 17.3 per cent.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The concerns also extended to AI infrastructure companies. Nvidia-backed cloud computing firms CoreWeave and Nebius saw their shares fall 8.8 per cent and 9 per cent, respectively, on November 13.The interconnected nature of the industry explains this. Nvidia supplies chips, cloud companies purchase computing capacity, data-centre operators build infrastructure and AI developers use them to train and run their models. Thus, a problem in one part of this chain can affect the others.Is AI spending sustainable?Technology companies are increasingly investing in data centres, advanced chips and energy infrastructure. However, the returns on these investments are still unclear and in many cases creating more fear than optimism, around steady revenue and growth.Another concern is circular financing, where companies investing in AI firms are also their customers or infrastructure providers. These deals help startups access computing power and give infrastructure providers a steady stream of business. However, they also raise questions about how much of the demand is coming from independent customers.Krishna Dev Pathak, investment banker and advisor to early-stage startups, said such arrangements are not necessarily unusual. "Much of what is described as circular financing is a familiar practice at an unfamiliar scale. Suppliers in many industries have long helped their customers buy from them. Nvidia backs AI labs and cloud providers, through investments and support for their data centre commitments, so they can build sooner and use its chips."The bigger concern, he added, is whether applications will generate enough paying customers to justify the infrastructure being built. "Where I would stay watchful is the gap between how fast infrastructure is being built and how fast paying applications are arriving."This gap could become particularly important for smaller companies that depend on external funding and expensive computing resources. If commercial revenues take longer to materialise, borrowing costs and infrastructure commitments could put pressure on their finances.Thus, Pathak believes the model can work, but more measured investment and funding linked to actual customer demand could ultimately benefit the industry.AI industry beyond Nvidia?A vulnerability is the concentration of computing infrastructure around Nvidia. Its customers do not simply purchase chips; they build software, applications and entire computing systems around the company's technology.This creates significant switching costs. Even if competing chipmakers offer alternatives, migrating existing systems can require substantial engineering work, time and investment.Atul Rai, co-founder and CEO of Staqu Technologies, says this dependence extends across Nvidia's technology ecosystem."Nvidia's dominance represents a genuine concentration risk for the global AI ecosystem. The dependency goes beyond GPUs. Its CUDA software ecosystem, developer tools and optimised libraries have created an entire technology stack around Nvidia hardware,” he said.However, not every AI workload requires the same computing power. Training advanced foundational models demands enormous processing capacity, while running AI applications, known as inference, offers greater scope for alternative chips and specialised processors.Cloud providers and technology companies are therefore exploring ways to diversify their computing requirements, reduce costs and avoid depending on a single supplier.A disruption to Nvidia could raise computing costs and delay data-centre projects. But Rai believes it could also accelerate a shift towards more efficient AI. "I don't believe such a disruption would stop the AI revolution. It would accelerate a transition that the industry already needs: moving from brute-force computation towards efficient, task-specific intelligence."For India, this could create opportunities in specialised AI models, efficient computing and applications built around real-world datasets. "The real moat in AI will increasingly be proprietary data, domain expertise and the ability to deliver intelligence economically, not simply access to the largest GPU clusters,” he added.Not just a corporate crisisOne more topic, a bit away from the standard financial and economic analysis, that has come up is the US-China technology rivalry. Washington has imposed restrictions on their exports to China, citing national security concerns.Amid those curbs, allegations involving Alice Huang and her reported association with Singapore-based Megaspeed renewed questions about whether restricted chips could reach China through third countries.Any expansion of scrutiny around chip transfers could have consequences for semiconductor companies, suppliers and countries involved in global technology supply chains. It could also lead to tighter compliance requirements and greater scrutiny of business relationships.Shristi Chaudhari, senior executive for regulatory intelligence and market research at Bureau Veritas, with a developing specialisation in geoeconomic analysis, said the controversy could bring greater attention to export controls, corporate governance and technology transfers.However, a setback for Nvidia does not automatically mean the US will lose its technological leadership. "The US has a much wider innovation ecosystem, supported by semiconductor research, cloud infrastructure, leading technology firms and substantial R&D investment."The developments could nevertheless accelerate China's efforts to strengthen its domestic chip industry. India, Japan and European economies may also seek to diversify their semiconductor supply chains.Complete technological independence, however, is unlikely given the complexity of global manufacturing."The more probable outcome is a diversification of supply chains and technology partnerships, where countries balance strategic autonomy with international cooperation rather than move towards complete technological isolation,” Chaudhari added.For India, this could create opportunities in semiconductor supply chains and data-centre investments, although access to capital, energy and advanced technology will remain challenges.Read more: Nvidia scandal just the tip of the iceberg? How China's spy machine plays a bigger gameWhat it means for overall AI growthFor investors, the burning question right now is whether the latest developments represent a temporary bout of volatility or a deeper reassessment of AI valuations.The technology sector had already been facing pressure over the scale of infrastructure investments and the debt being used to finance them. The uncertainty surrounding Nvidia has given investors another reason to reassess their exposure to companies whose valuations depend heavily on future AI demand.Harsha Vardhana VM, founder and group CEO of Atom Financial Services, says the timing of the developments is significant because markets were already under pressure."The Nasdaq saw a peak on October 6 this year and has been on a slide down ever since. Doubts are arising about the massive debt funding data centers across the world and the not-so-great returns expected from AI projects that have taken centrestage on market sentiment,” he said.He believes the Nvidia developments gave already nervous investors another reason to reduce exposure to technology stocks. However, he does not see the controversy bringing down the entire AI investment theme."Collapsing of an entire theme because a single founder's PR failed is quite a long shot,” he added.Instead, investors could become more selective, reassessing companies whose valuations depend heavily on future AI demand. Competitors could also benefit if cloud providers diversify their chip purchases.Sandesh Sharda, founder of Gro More Portfolio Management LLC and Titan-Ideabaaz, also shared his view that corporate controversies and leadership changes may create temporary volatility without derailing a larger technological transition."Every major technology shift goes through a settlement phase just as we saw with the dot-com era, the transition from iPods to iPads, and wired phones to wireless,” he said.He further pointed to AI's expanding applications in medical sciences, drug discovery, software services and real estate as reasons the broader technology trend is likely to continue.Also read: The technology China wants and America won't shareWhat nextInvestors will be watching Nvidia's leadership changes, US export policies and whether major customers start buying chips from other suppliers. The company's earnings, expected on Tuesday (Wednesday IST), will also be closely watched. More broadly, the sustainability of spending on AI infrastructure will remain a key concern.The controversy has highlighted how dependent the AI industry is on just a handful of companies for now. However, looking at challenges beyond one company’s internal issues, tech firms will have to show that their massive investments in chips and data centres can generate steady returns.That said, Nvidia's market dominance is difficult to overlook. With a new interim CEO at the helm, investors will be watching how effectively the company can maintain its technological relevance, reassure customers and restore confidence in its business at a time when the wider AI industry is already under scrutiny.Ultimately, in an overall outlook, investors need signs that the AI industry can deliver sustainable growth.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mobuoy: Dump clean-up could cost £161m over 30 years, says environment minister
articles.summary: Environment Minister Andrew Muir has described what happened at Mobuoy, near Derry, as an "absolute scandal" which could take a generation to fix.
articles.body:
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.

The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.

Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.

Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.

Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".

He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.

Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.

Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.

The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.

The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.

"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .

The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.

"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."

Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.

"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.

"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."

Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.

Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.

One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

articles.title: West Virginia's state auditor has been indicted after prosecutors alleged he overrode staff objections to issue tax deeds for nine properties to benefit a friend, allegedly taking land from its rightful owners
articles.summary: West Virginia State Auditor Mark A. Hunt faces federal indictment for allegedly overriding staff objections to facilitate tax-delinquent property transfers for a friend, alongside serious allegations of fraud and misconduct involving state employees.
articles.body: West Virginia State Auditor Mark A. Hunt has been indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations that he used his office to help a longtime friend and business associate obtain nine tax-delinquent properties, overriding objections from staff who said the transfers were not legally permitted.Hunt, 66, is among four men charged with nine counts of theft of property in connection with the alleged scheme. The indictment also names two senior officials from the auditor's office and a state employee in separate allegations involving falsified government timecards and bank fraud.US Attorney Moore Capito announced the charges, saying the investigation concerned the alleged misuse of public office for personal benefit.Why the nine property transfers are under investigationThe properties are located in Kanawha and Boone counties and were being sought by a business entity associated with Robert Lisle Johns, 66, described by prosecutors as Hunt's longtime friend and business associate.Employees in the auditor's Land Division determined that all nine properties were ineligible for deed issuance because the purchaser had failed to make the required payments and submit paperwork within statutory deadlines, according to the indictment.Prosecutors allege Hunt proceeded despite these objections. He personally signed deeds for eight properties on March 28 last year followed by the ninth on June 6. Hunt had taken office in January that year.The indictment alleges that Hunt was assisted by David Keith Cole, the deputy chief of staff in the auditor's office, and Frederic Scott Caudill, its general counsel. Johns was appointed special counsel to the office in June 2025.Prosecutors allege the four men were involved in the issuance of the deeds, resulting in the properties being taken from their lawful owners.Separate bank fraud allegations involve state employeeThe grand jury also indicted Hunt and Cole alongside Marie Ann Hoffmann, 66, an employee of the state auditor's office, in a separate bank fraud case.According to prosecutors, Hoffmann submitted falsified government timecards that included hours she had spent working at Hunt's private law firm, Mark A. Hunt & Associates. The alleged arrangement ran from May 5, to at least September 29 this year.Hoffmann was a full-time state employee who left her government duty station on Friday afternoons to perform paralegal and administrative work at the private firm. Hunt and Cole also frequently worked with her there during state business hours, according to the indictment.Cole approved the falsified timecards, enabling Hoffmann to receive wages from the West Virginia Treasury for work she had not performed for the state auditor's office. Hunt was aware of the arrangement, according to prosecutors.Two officials face additional charges over FBI interviewsCole and Caudill have each been charged with making materially false statements to federal investigators during interviews concerning the disputed property deeds.Caudill allegedly made false statements during an FBI interview on October 26 including about whether he had asked staff who would act as a whistleblower over the handling of the deeds.Cole is accused of making false statements during an October 6 interview about the property transfers and his approval of Hoffmann's timecards.The theft charges carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. Making materially false statements to federal investigators carries a maximum five-year prison term, while bank fraud carries up to 30 years in prison and a fine of up to $1 million.West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack called for Hunt's resignation following the indictment, saying the allegations required serious attention and that residents deserved transparency and accountability from elected officials.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mumbai's ageing offices hold Rs 1.78 lakh crore value opportunity, modernising 68 million sq ft of commercial space could nearly double its valuation from Rs 1.86 lakh crore to Rs 3.63 lakh crore
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Mumbai's ageing commercial buildings could become a major source of fresh value for the property market, with modernisation of existing offices
articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai's ageing commercial buildings could become a major source of fresh value for the property market, with modernisation of existing offices potentially unlocking an additional Rs 1.78 lakh crore in asset value, a new Knight Frank India report has estimated. The Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) has 68 million sq ft of office stock eligible for retrofitting, whose combined valuation could rise from Rs 1.86 lakh crore to Rs 3.63 lakh crore — a potential 96% increase.The opportunity is particularly significant in a city where premium commercial locations are increasingly difficult to replicate and redevelopment can entail substantial costs, regulatory processes and operational disruption. Upgrading existing buildings could help owners command better rentals and attract institutional and corporate occupiers without having to demolish and rebuild.The report, Age to Advantage: Retrofitting India's Office Stock, estimates that 301 million sq ft, or 28% of the total 1.076 billion sq ft office inventory across India's top eight markets, is suitable for such interventions. The value of this stock could rise 76%, from Rs 4.96 lakh crore to Rs 8.72 lakh crore, creating Rs 3.76 lakh crore in incremental asset value.Mumbai's suburban offices offer bigger opportunityA striking finding is that Mumbai's suburban business districts (SBDs) account for a much larger share of the region's retrofitting opportunity than its central business districts (CBDs).Across MMR, eligible SBD office stock is valued at Rs 1.49 lakh crore currently and could reach Rs 2.91 lakh crore after modernisation, translating into an estimated 95% increase and Rs 1.42 lakh crore in additional value. In comparison, eligible CBD stock could rise from Rs 36,600 crore to Rs 72,100 crore, a 97% increase.The CBD opportunity is concentrated in established commercial locations such as Nariman Point and Fort, while the SBD analysis captures the value potential across Mumbai's suburban business corridors.Nationally, the retrofitting opportunity in CBDs is estimated at Rs 1.45 lakh crore, with a 70% potential valuation increase. SBDs offer an even larger Rs 2.31 lakh crore opportunity, with an estimated 80% increase.Ageing buildings meet tightening office supplyThe case for modernising existing offices is strengthened by the age profile of India's commercial real estate. Around 34% of the country's office stock was developed before 2010, including 3% built before 2000.At the same time, the ratio of new office completions to absorption — an indicator of the balance between fresh supply and occupier demand — has fallen from 1.40 in 2008 to 0.73 in the first nine months of 2026.India has approximately 1.076 billion sq ft of office space, making it the world's fourth-largest office market by stock. However, Grade A properties account for only 56%, or around 603 million sq ft. Retrofitting could help bridge this quality gap by upgrading existing buildings to meet contemporary workplace, safety, technology and sustainability requirements.The interventions could include modernising air-conditioning, electrical and plumbing systems, façades, lifts, lobbies, parking, fire safety, digital connectivity, security and accessibility.The opportunity varies considerably across markets. NCR has the largest retrofit-eligible stock by volume at 81 million sq ft, representing 39% of its inventory, with an estimated 82% valuation upside. Ahmedabad has the highest proportion of ageing stock eligible for upgrading at 63%, while Bengaluru, despite being India's largest office market by volume, has only 12% eligible stock."Modernising these legacy assets represents a great opportunity for developers and asset owners to unlock value while strengthening asset competitiveness and attracting quality occupiers," said Shishir Baijal, chairman and managing director, Knight Frank India.Deben Moza, senior executive director and head of project management services for India and APAC at Knight Frank India, said energy efficiency, digital infrastructure, safety and occupant experience would increasingly become strategic priorities for office owners, particularly as corporates place greater emphasis on sustainability and ESG commitments.The report's valuation projections are based on assumptions of higher achievable rentals and lower capitalisation rates for retrofitted properties. The estimated appreciation is therefore a potential market-value gain, not a guaranteed return or a measure of net profit after renovation expenditure.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.summary: The new rules restrict chip exports and also access to their computing power, which China relies on heavily.
articles.body:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title: Why are five EU countries reviving plans to deport migrants to Rwanda?
articles.summary: Rwanda again proposed as a ‘return hub’ for deported migrants, but critics warn of potential human rights abuses.
articles.body:
Five European Union countries have announced a deal with Rwanda under which it is set to host rejected asylum seekers.

On Monday, Rwanda joined Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing the scheme in Vienna, with a plan to begin transfers by 2027.

The governments say the deal would speed up the removal of people with no right to remain in Europe, while rights groups say it could expose vulnerable people to abuse.

The five governments want to establish a “return hub” in Rwanda – a facility outside the EU where migrants ordered to leave member states can be transferred, even if they are not from Rwanda.

The proposed scheme would apply only to people in the five countries who are subject to enforceable removal orders, including rejected asylum seekers. The governments would cover the costs, including temporary accommodation.

According to a joint statement, those transferred “will have the opportunity to integrate into the society of Rwanda”. Alternatively, they could voluntarily return to their home country or travel to another country they can legally enter, with assistance from Rwanda and international organisations.

A formal agreement has yet to be signed, and the governments have not specified how many people they intend to transfer. There were 669,365 first-time asylum applications across the EU in 2025, according to figures from the European Commission. On average, 45 percent of these are approved. However, European officials said last year that about 90 percent of rejected applicants remain in the bloc overall.

Dutch Deputy Prime Minister Bart van den Brink said Rwanda was chosen for its “considerable experience” in receiving large groups of migrants and its close cooperation with the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

Rwanda has long hosted large numbers of refugees, most of them from the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo and Burundi.

But over the years, it has also cut deals with several governments to receive deportees. Between 2013 and 2018, Israel deported thousands of Eritrean and Sudanese migrants to Rwanda under a secretive deal.

Rwanda received another 3,000 migrants transferred from Libya in a deal with UNHCR and the African Union in 2019. Last year, Rwanda agreed to accept hundreds of deportees from the United States, with the first seven arriving later that month.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the new scheme would offer people with no right to remain in Europe a “second chance”.

A background paper released on Sunday envisions a “cost-efficient and sustainable model”, in which the five EU states would cover the hub’s direct costs and fund integration and migrant welfare projects they say would also benefit Rwandans and aid the country’s development.

The joint statement says the arrangement would form part of an “equal and mutually beneficial partnership” between Rwanda and the five countries, covering not only migration but other areas of common interest.

Yes, but that deal, signed in 2022 by the former ruling Conservative government, went a bit further than this. Rather than transferring people after their asylum claims had failed in the United Kingdom, all asylum seekers who arrived in the UK “irregularly” were to be transferred to Rwanda to have their claims assessed there. Those granted asylum would be resettled in Rwanda rather than the UK.

In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled the plan unlawful, finding that those transferred would face a real risk of refoulement – being forcibly returned to countries where they could face abuse.

UNHCR, which opposed the plan, told UK courts that Rwanda’s asylum system was inadequate to receive the asylum seekers, among other objections relating to safety and human rights.

The scheme was eventually scrapped in 2024 after the UK’s Labour Party came to power, though by then London had paid Rwanda about 290 million pounds ($390m) under the scheme. Only four people had relocated to Rwanda, all voluntarily.

Under the latest scheme, the five EU states say they would only transfer people who have already been legally processed for asylum and found not to need protection.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said this difference made the two plans “incomparable”.

UNHCR, which challenged the aborted UK scheme in courts, is now advising Rwanda and the five EU governments on whether this new plan complies with international human rights law.

Rights groups have objected to the plan despite Rwanda’s promise of independent monitoring and UNHCR’s involvement, objecting to third-country deportations, in principle, and to Rwanda’s human rights record.

A coalition of 47 groups, including the International Rescue Committee, warned that the deal means people could be torn away from lives built in Europe to countries where they may have no family or networks.

The coalition pointed to the experience of asylum seekers whom Israel deported to Rwanda. “When Israel deported people to Rwanda and Uganda, they were promised status and safety. But research indicates that many were driven on to dangerous onward journeys and into the hands of human trafficking networks,” the coalition said.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) opposed the deal, saying that such third-country transfers were documented to lead to abuses for the deportees, including “arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, destitution” and other serious abuses.

“History has shown that third-country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said HRW’s Judith Sunderland.

Amnesty International said similar schemes in the past had proven “unlawful, unworkable and expensive”.

Rights organisations also point to Rwanda’s human rights record as cause for concern. In its report for 2025, Amnesty International wrote of Rwanda: “Forced evictions associated with urban development projects in the capital disproportionately affected low-income and marginalised populations. Labour rights protections were limited, and structural barriers impeded trade union activity. Civic space remained severely restricted and political opposition members faced unfair prosecution.”

HRW said the scheme to send failed asylum seekers would fall short of the EU’s requirement that partner countries respect international human rights law.

The rights group added that four of the five EU countries involved in the deal had raised concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record at the United Nations just this January.

articles.title: Who is behind Habibi UK, an X account that targeted critics of Israel?
articles.summary: A former US Foreign Service officer ran a company that funded election adverts attacking Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour.
articles.body:
The anonymous X account Habibi UK branded opponents of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza “racists”, “hate marchers” and “anti-Semites”, singling out politicians, broadcasters and campaigners for online attacks.

A six-month investigation by the British publication Byline Times has now identified the person behind the account as Benjamin Tait, a 61-year-old former United States Foreign Service officer who went on to run a British energy research company.

The news website and newspaper said that since the initial part of its investigation was published on Thursday, the account has stopped posting.

The account, which joined what was then Twitter in April 2015, used a coronation portrait of Queen Elizabeth I as its profile picture, gave its location as “The Realm” and quoted a line attributed to the monarch in its bio: “If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.”

An analysis of nearly 300,000 X posts placed @habibi_uk at the centre of a network of 13 anonymous accounts. It found that Habibi UK had posted more than 42,000 times.

The investigation also documented campaigns against 12 public figures in Britain over 10 months. Among those targeted were former BBC presenter and professional footballer Gary Lineker, photographer and outgoing chairman of London’s Southbank Centre arts centre Misan Harriman, documentary filmmaker Louis Theroux, actor and television panellist Nadia Sawalha and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. All of them had spoken out against Israel’s actions against Palestinians.

Tait, a British-American grandson of philosopher Bertrand Russell, graduated from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service in Washington, DC. According to his LinkedIn profile, which has now been taken down, Tait spent two years as a US Department of State officer overseas with experience in political-military diplomacy and “counterterrorism research”.

Tait and his wife ran Prospex Research for about three decades. It was a firm that produced energy market reports for clients, including banks, consultancies, government officials and law firms. Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones quoted Tait on energy markets. The company entered voluntary liquidation in September.

Tait was writing under the name Habibi by at least 2008 on Harry’s Place, a British political blog that began as a centre-left forum. His early posts focused on alleged “Islamist extremism”, including pieces about campaigner Ismail Patel and the Palestinian aid charity Interpal, according to the investigation.

What was Tait’s role in campaign against Jeremy Corbyn?

Before the United Kingdom’s 2019 general election, Tait was the sole director and controlling owner of MTCAE Ltd, according to Companies House records cited by the Byline Times. The company ran Mainstream, a campaign registered to spend money during the elections independently of a political party.

Mainstream was founded and chaired by Ian Austin, a former Labour MP who quit the party under Jeremy Corbyn and has served as Britain’s trade envoy to Israel under five prime ministers. Austin said the group was set up to oppose “extremism” on the far left and hard right. But the Byline Times found that the Facebook advertisements it examined all attacked the Labour Party, including one that portrayed Corbyn as a national security threat.

Electoral Commission returns showed the company spent £134,457 pounds ($171,715) on the campaign, including 6,880 pounds ($8,786) paid to Tait for overhead costs and administration. The returns listed no donor.

In March 2021, a High Court official ordered Twitter to disclose details behind the account to Professor David Miller, who had brought a legal claim. The operator’s name remained out of the public record. Despite this, the account went on to gain influence, particularly after Elon Musk took over Twitter in October 2022.

Links between the account and the Labour Party establishment run deep, according to the investigation. Austin, who is connected to Tait via Mainstream, shared posts from Habibi UK at least 34 times. John Woodcock, a former Labour MP who sits in the House of Lords, amplified the account 32 times, according to the investigation. It also found that David Toube, general counsel at the Jewish Leadership Council, amplified its posts hundreds of times.

The Henry Jackson Society, a British foreign policy think tank, cited Habibi UK nine times in a 2022 report on Hindu-Muslim unrest in Leicester.

articles.title: Drinking 6 to 8 cups of tea a day linked to lower risk of serious diseases, massive study finds
articles.summary: A Journal of Internal Medicine study of nearly 486,000 adults links consistent tea drinking to an 11% lower risk of vascular disease overall.
articles.body: Drinking six to eight cups of tea a day could help lower the risk of vascular disease, according to a recent study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine. The study, which was conducted in China, involved 485,934 adult participants. After a median follow-up period of 9.05 years, researchers identified 14,863 cases of cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, pulmonary heart disease and peripheral artery disease among participants. LIVING LONGER MAY START WITH 3 FOODS A DOCTOR EATS EVERY DAY Consistent tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of those diseases. Those who drank approximately six to eight cups of tea each day were found to have the lowest risk of developing vascular diseases. Smoking and physical activity levels were also taken into account. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Participants who did not smoke, were physically active and drank tea regularly had the lowest risk of developing vascular diseases. Tea strength also affected the results, researchers found. The study does not specify what exactly "tea strength" means in this case, but it's possible that the term refers to caffeine content. Moderate-strength tea was linked with the lowest risk of vascular disease, while strong tea was linked to an increased risk of developing vascular disease. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Those who drank black tea had more consistent negative correlations with vascular disease than those who drank green tea. "Both black and green tea contain polyphenols, including flavonoids, which are plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties," Amy Davis, a San Diego, California-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "These compounds may help support healthy blood vessel function and blood pressure, which are important factors in cardiovascular health." "Drinking unsweetened tea can also help you stay hydrated without any added sugar or artificial ingredients," Davis added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The study's conclusion states that its findings "support considering multidimensional tea-drinking and lifestyle patterns in vascular health research." A study published in 2024 examining the correlation between tea consumption and life expectancy found that participants who drank three to five cups of tea daily had a life expectancy increase of 2.24 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Very few long-term studies have looked at the effects of tea on heart disease risk. However, the limited evidence currently available suggests that both green and black tea might have beneficial effects on some heart disease risk factors, including blood pressure and cholesterol," according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: New York's gutted police unit was more than a protest squad
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani is dissolving the NYPD Strategic Response Group for a civilian-led de-escalation plan critics say will embolden criminals and terrorists.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is dissolving the NYPD's Strategic Response Group — an elite tactical unit criticized for its handling of some left-wing protests while also responding to critical threats including a mass shooting at an office building last year and an attempted bombing attack on dueling demonstrations outside the city's mayoral residence. "I think it’s one more step towards emboldening the criminals, emboldening the anarchists and emboldening the terrorists," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and Fox News contributor who spent years working alongside the NYPD. Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists. MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS "New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news briefing announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation." List of prominent incidents involving SRG going back to the George Floyd protests in 2020: The mayor plans to replace the SRG with several new programs by next spring. First is an unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). This civilian team won't have arrest authority. It will work with a new First Amendment Support Team (FAST), consisting of 30 uniformed officers with specialized training in communication and de-escalation, according to Mamdani's office. Lastly, his overhaul includes the creation of a new Patrol Support Division consisting of officers who will be trained in crowd control but spend most of their time on patrol duties. Counterterrorism duties will be consolidated in the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau. MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE But the SRG has a varied role. While members are on hand for crowd control at large demonstrations, they also protect the protesters from outside threats. And they are positioned at other events involving large crowds, including the city's many parades, the iconic New Year's ball drop and other large events that take place every year. "What the Strategic Response Group was designed to do was to be a highly mobile, well-trained, well-equipped group, like a senior SWAT team," Gagliano told Fox News Digital. Unlike the NYPD's SWAT team, known as its Emergency Services Unit, the SRG also has a public-facing role, Gagliano said. "Part of that was being on the front lines, the deterrent effect, and I think that's something that we're losing as well," he said. ALLEGED ISIS-INSPIRED TERROR SUSPECTS LEFT FEDS ‘VOLUMINOUS’ DIGITAL TRAIL, FAMILY BREAKS DOWN IN TEARS Terrorists and other criminals targeting public events tend to pick soft targets and the path of least resistance, he added. "The Strategic Response Group was a deterrent, and it probably caused some people to decide, ‘Yeah, I’m not gonna try that. I’m not gonna do that,'" he said. POLICE GROUPS CONDEMN MAMDANI OVER AXING ELITE NYPD UNIT The unit has also been deployed around large public events with the goal of responding rapidly when needed, Gagliano said. "The uniform folks are there for a deterrent effect," he said. "The uniform folks kept in abeyance like SRG, that are rolled out quickly and mobilized and strategically placed so that they can get to different spots very quickly." MAMDANI’S FIRST 100-PLUS DAYS: FAR-LEFT MAYOR FLUNKS A KEY LEADERSHIP TEST Vincent J. Vallelong, president of the NYPD Sergeants Benevolent Association, brought up the failed Gracie Mansion bombing Monday. "When an alleged terrorist attack threatened lives near Gracie Mansion, NYPD Sgt. Luis Navarro and Chief Aaron Edwards ran toward danger," Vallelong said in a statement. "Their decisive actions should be a lesson for Mayor Mamdani." HAMAS, HEZBOLLAH FLAGS FLY AT ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST MINUTES AFTER MAMDANI CONDEMNS TERROR PLOT AGAINST JEWS Two allegedly ISIS-inspired men, Emir Balat and Ibrahim Kayumi, were arrested after federal prosecutors say they threw improvised explosive devices at a crowd outside the mayor's home and at a group of police as left- and right-wing protesters demonstrated across from one another. The bombs failed to explode. According to federal prosecutors, Balat allegedly told police he had wanted the attack to be "bigger" than the Boston Marathon Bombing, which killed three and injured hundreds in 2013. MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES The SRG also deployed to help search for the gunman floor-by-floor after the mass shooting inside a Manhattan office building that houses the NFL’s headquarters on Park Avenue. SEND US A TIP Vallelong scoffed at the idea that the unarmed CDDD will protect the public from similar violent plots. "Unarmed civilians cannot talk a determined attacker out of detonating a bomb," he said. "I fear this approach will embolden violent agitators to infiltrate peaceful demonstrations, putting protesters, police and bystanders at risk." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027, he said. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.

articles.title: State Department presses Egypt to respect religious freedom as Christian convert faces possible execution
articles.summary: The State Department is pressing Egypt to protect religious freedom as a Christian convert faces possible execution or 25 years in prison, raising concerns over his trial.
articles.body: The State Department has intensified its efforts to compel the majority Muslim state of Egypt to honor the religious liberty protections for an Egyptian who converted to Christianity and is facing either the death penalty or a lengthy prison term. The prosecution of Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek has catapulted his case and has attracted publicity within the U.S., Britain and across the global Christian community. Egypt receives $1.3 billion in annual funding from the U.S. In July, Fox News Digital reported on Abdelrazek’s trial for his embrace of Christianity in 2016. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that, "We are monitoring his trial closely. Religious freedom is a fundamental human value, and we encourage the Egyptian government to protect the religious freedom rights of all its citizens." The situation for Abdelrazek has become dire, according to his attorney and human rights advocates for Coptic Christians in Egypt. He faces execution or a 25-year prison sentence for his conversion to Christianity, according to the office of his lawyer, Said Fayez. Fayez’s office said that in early November the "Public Prosecution presented its closing arguments and requested that the maximum penalty prescribed by law be imposed upon him." PAKISTAN’S TOP COURT UPHOLDS CHRISTIAN MAN’S DEATH SENTENCE FOR BLASPHEMY Fox News Digital reached out multiple times to Egypt’s Embassy in Washington, D.C., and its Foreign Ministry for a comment. According to Amnesty International, in "July 2025, security officers arrested Egyptian national and Christian convert Said Abdelrazek from his home in Cairo. After nine months of arbitrary pretrial detention, Said Abdelrazek was referred to trial before the Terrorism Circuit of the First Criminal Court in Badr on charges stemming from his conversion and religious beliefs." Coptic Solidarity reported he faces charges that include contempt for Islam, and inciting unrest and spreading false information. Abdelrazek’s fiancée Sophia, an Australian-Egyptian citizen, has been energetically campaigning to secure his freedom. She told Fox News Digital that she is "pleading for them to release him." She declined to use her last name because of "some extreme threats" against her. Lindsay Rodriguez, a spokeswoman for Coptic Solidarity, told Fox News Digital that "Coptic Solidarity is deeply concerned that Egyptian prosecutors are seeking the maximum penalty against Said Abdelrazek, a Christian convert whose case has become an important test of religious freedom and judicial impartiality in Egypt." She continued that he "has been detained since July 2025 and is being prosecuted before a terrorism court, primarily on an allegation of joining a banned terrorist organization, as well as charges of contempt for Islam, inciting unrest and spreading false information. These remain prosecution allegations, not findings of guilt. His defense will present its closing arguments on Dec. 8. Reported religious remarks attributed to the judge during the Nov. 3 hearing further heighten concerns about whether a Christian convert can receive a genuinely impartial hearing." His supporters say the prosecution has yet to name the terrorist organization in question while noting there is no known terrorist group associated with Christians listed in Egypt. Rodriguez added that "Peaceful religious conversion and expression must not be treated as terrorism or national-security offenses. The United States, European Union and Australia should use the Dec. 8 hearing as a clear test of Egypt's willingness to uphold basic religious-freedom and fair-trial standards." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rodriguez said, "The U.S. Embassy in Cairo, EU Delegation and Member State embassies should seek access to monitor the hearing and raise Said's case directly with Egyptian authorities. Members of Congress and the European Parliament should publicly demonstrate that they are following the case. Australia also has a particular responsibility: Said's fiancée is an Australian citizen, and DFAT [Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] should press his case while Home Affairs ensures a viable humanitarian pathway for reunification upon his release." The Egyptian Christian community makes up an estimated 10% of the nation’s 120 million people.

articles.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
articles.summary: The Singapore-based company is suspected of helping to ship high-end AI chips from tech giant Nvidia to China, violating US export rules.
articles.body:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

articles.title: Grassroots student movement takes control as Serbia’s new parliament convenes
articles.summary: Serbia’s new parliament met for the first time since the stunning election victory by a grassroots student-led movement that ousted President Aleksandar Vucic.
articles.body: Serbia’s new parliament met on Tuesday for the first time since the stunning election victory last month by a grassroots student-led movement that ousted then President Aleksandar Vucic and his party. The National Assembly’s inaugural session marks the first step toward the formation of Serbia’s new government. It’s also the first time ever in the Balkan country that a newly-formed protest movement makes up the parliamentary majority. The lawmakers are set first to choose a parliamentary speaker, his or her deputies and various assembly bodies. A new government then must be voted into office within 90 days. The Students’ List movement holds 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 103 belonging to Vucic’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party. Vucic himself is now one of the opposition lawmakers after serving as defense minister, prime minister and president over the past 14 years. The remaining parliamentary seats belong to the parties of Serbia’s ethnic minorities. Hundreds of people gathered outside the parliament building in central Belgrade to see off the student-backed lawmakers, who are mostly teachers, professors and other experts with respected careers but little or no political experience. Serbian media have reported that the lawmakers spent days practicing and preparing for the session, where they will face well-versed and experienced opposition lawmakers notorious for aggressive verbal attacks on opponents. The Students’ List group on Oct. 25 defeated Vucic’s right-wing SNS in the early parliamentary vote that came after two years of anti-corruption protests in the Balkan country. The SNS party’s caretaker government remains in office until a new Cabinet is confirmed. Serbia also must hold an early presidential election by the end of the year. The date for the vote has yet to be determined. It was triggered by Vucic’s resignation in September as president to pursue a failed attempt to become the new prime minister. The protests erupted first in November 2024 in response to a train station tragedy, which involved the collapse of a concrete canopy, in Serbia’s north that killed 16 people. Many in Serbia blamed the collapse on flawed renovation work and rampant graft. Students have promised to restore democracy and the rule of law, and to terminate deeply rooted corruption, cronyism and alleged organized crime links that they say thrived under Vucic. Observers have predicted that the Students’ List group will face resistance within the system, and strong opposition in parliament. The students have said they won’t allow the session to turn into a “reality show.” The parliamentary meeting’s live coverage on the state-run RTS television station is expected to be widely watched. Some bars in Belgrade and elsewhere in Serbia advertised special prices for people to watch it. Vucic has accused the students of “revolutionary terror” in daily appearances on loyal media and social networks following a surge in postelection arrests that included officials, police officers and a private bank owner who allegedly attempted to siphon off money. Serbia is a candidate nation for European Union membership, but the effort has stalled under Vucic because of democratic backsliding and close ties with Russia. EU officials have offered to help the future Serbian government through the promised reforms.

articles.title: Rebeca Grynspan could be the UN’s first woman boss, if she can sway Trump
articles.summary: Swaying the US could test Grynspan but she likes taking risks – and wants UN to take more, she tells Al Jazeera.
articles.body:
In straw poll after straw poll among members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) to choose the organisation’s next leader, one name keeps emerging ahead of all others: Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.

If Grynspan, 70, beats out the other candidates, the current head of the UN’s top trade body would become the world’s first woman and the first Jewish person to hold the post of UN secretary-general.

But as the December 31 deadline to pick UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres ‘ successor rapidly approaches, Grynspan continues to struggle to convert her frontrunner status into a win, because of at least one veto against her candidature.

With secret ballots , geopolitical rivalries and multiple – eight in all – candidates vying for the world’s top diplomatic job, there is no public confirmation of just which of the five permanent members of the UNSC are opposed to Grynspan’s election.

Yet her background as a UN insider, and her work on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory and Russia’s war on Ukraine, mean that Grynspan carries baggage that she will need to overcome in order to win the support of the world’s most powerful nations, say analysts. And she’ll need to win over one leader above all, who has demonstrated his desire to dismantle the very UN Grynspan hopes to lead: United States President Donald Trump.

What she has going for her, though, she says, is a track record of diplomacy – and a willingness to take risks, herself, and for the organisation.

“The UN must become less risk-averse. Its biggest risk today is the risk of not trying,” she told Al Jazeera. “I have listened to people who need the UN but increasingly doubt it can act. They want leadership willing to take risks for peace.”

The current chief of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the former vice president of Costa Rica acknowledged that diplomatic negotiations don’t always work – at least at first. But that, she argued, only makes the UN chief’s job that much more important.

“Any mediator knows that 10 ideas may fail before the 11th succeeds,” she said. “Few governments can afford the political cost of so many rejections. The secretary-general can.”

A past spanning Costa Rica, Latin America and beyond

Grynspan is no stranger to the “first” label – she became UNCTAD’s first woman secretary-general when she was appointed to the role in 2021. She took on its reins, promising post-COVID economic recovery, supporting digital transitions, and aligning with UN goals on climate change.

But before this post, Grynspan held a long career in Latin American politics and international diplomacy, including as second vice president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998.

An economist by trade, her various government ministerial positions included at one time being deputy finance minister, where she played a key role in the country’s debt crisis in the eighties.

After years of government experience, she took on roles beyond Costa Rica. In 2014, she was appointed as the secretary-general of the Ibero-American Conference by the bloc’s 22 nations spanning Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe. She has also held leading roles within the UN Development Programme (UNDP), as well as the UN Commission for the Reconstruction of Haiti.

In her bid for UN secretary-general, Grynspan has laid out her vision of reform of the international body, and says she would push for the UN to take a more active role in negotiations to end wars.

“To defend the United Nations today is to have the courage to change it. No organisation after 80 years can say, we don’t have to change anything,” the frontrunner said to Al Jazeera.

“The UN has to embrace reform, not be defensive about reform.”

As head of UNCTAD, Grynspan has spearheaded the organisation’s work on global trade, debt, and economic inequality.

She is widely credited with having played an important role in the UN’s Black Sea Grain Initiative, which facilitated Ukrainian agricultural exports through the Black Sea during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. She negotiated that deal between the warring parties while undergoing breast cancer treatment.

“Making the agreements work meant bringing others to the table,” Grynspan recalled. “Banks would not clear payments, insurers would not cover vessels and shipping companies hesitated. We brought them into the effort.”

According to UNCTAD, the UN and Turkiye-brokered initiative in 2022 exported 32 million tonnes of grain and lowered global food prices by 22 percent, before Russia withdrew from the deal a year later.

What made the deal work for a year before it collapsed, Grynspan said, was helping Russia and Ukraine understand that they did not have to agree about the war itself to make the grain agreement possible.

That’s the approach she says she will bring to the UNSC if she wins its top spot.

“If wars do not wait for ideal conditions, neither should diplomacy,” she said.

Grynspan’s previous criticisms of Russia’s withdrawal from the deal, however, could mean Moscow may veto her bid, Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, has previously told Al Jazeera.

But the frontrunner has been lobbying, like other candidates, to win the support of key UNSC member states, having met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in April.

The daughter of Polish Jewish refugees who fled to Central America during the Holocaust, Grynspan has close family ties to Israel. She studied there at one time, her sister has been living in the country for years, her nephew and niece served in the Israeli military, and her relatives there describe themselves as Zionists.

Her position on Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza , however, has broadly aligned with that of the UN: She condemned Hamas’s October 2023 attack and called for a ceasefire in Israel’s subsequent war on the besieged territory, which the UN’s independent Commission of Inquiry has found to constitute genocide.

During Grynspan’s time as UNCTAD chief, the organisation has published numerous reports warning that Israeli policies have ushered in the economic collapse of the Palestinian economy.

Its landmark report from February of this year found that “cumulatively, the Palestinian economy lost an estimated $212.2bn (in constant 2015 dollars) from 2000 to 2024.

“This partial, estimated lost potential, equivalent to nearly 20 times the entire Palestinian GDP of 2024, stems directly from Israeli occupation policies, restrictions, closures, and recurrent military operations,” the report stated.

Last year, Grynspan had called attention to the fact that Gaza’s gross domestic product per capita had plummeted to $161 per year – an 83 percent collapse from $970 in 2023 before the start of the genocide, among the most drastic economic contractions in modern history.

Her background, combined with her work, has therefore drawn attention from both sides of the Israel-Palestine conflict, despite her largely refraining from publicly commenting on it or her Jewish identity.

“What my identity gives me is empathy, not bias,” Grynspan said to Al Jazeera.

Speaking about her parents’ Jewish refugee experience, she emphasised the universal lessons that come from such displacement.

“I am the daughter of peace. My parents were refugees of the Second World War. I know what war takes away and I know what peace makes possible. It is possible for us to do it again, together,” said Grynspan.

According to Haaretz, Israeli officials have not publicly commented on Grynspan’s potential accession to UN Secretary-General.

Straw polls have placed Grynspan at the top of the field, but the five permanent members of the UNSC – the US, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom – each hold veto power, meaning opposition from any one of them could derail her candidacy.

With Grynspan seen as a dyed-in-the-wool UN insider, and Trump having repeatedly sought to weaken and reshape the organisation, analysts have questioned whether she can convince his administration that she is the right person to lead it.

Earlier this month, the US, alongside Russia, reportedly backed the UAE’s candidate, Lana Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.

Nusseibeh had six votes against her out of 15 members in the UNSC, per the latest straw poll earlier this month, but it is unclear whether those include any vetoes. China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.

According to Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) and a former US assistant secretary of state for international organisation affairs, Grynspan would have to demonstrate a commitment to “reform, reorganisation, and consolidation” of the UN system in order to appeal to Trump and garner US support.

“An insider candidate has to work much harder to convince decision-makers of her commitment to change such a large and complicated organisation,” Brimmer told Al Jazeera.

“US officials have been clear and consistent in highlighting the need for reform. Multilateral diplomacy will be shaped by how that ‘reform’ is defined and implemented.”

Whether Grynspan’s vision of reform matches that of Trump and his administration could determine if she secures the UN’s top job. She’s brokered difficult negotiations before, but Grynspan might be facing her toughest test yet.
