articles.title: ‘Frightened’ Texas neighbors left to wonder what political domino will fall next
articles.summary: Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana residents react to Texas flipping blue in the 2026 midterm election, fearing a chain reaction could reach red states.
articles.body: After the blue wave hit Texas in the 2026 midterm election, residents of neighboring red states are wondering whether their state could be next. Fox News Digital traveled to Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana to ask residents how they view the political shift in Texas and whether they think their state could flip in the near future. Residents in these states said the economy and protecting conservative values were among their top issues. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES Oklahoma Residents in the small town of Guthrie, Oklahoma, during a morning breakfast stop at Katie’s Diner, expressed concern about their southern neighbor electing Democrats, and believe that if it can happen in Texas, it can happen in the Sooner State. Roger from Guthrie said, "It's awful, isn't it? I blame it a lot on the Democrats when they let all those people cross the border." Stephanie from Guthrie shared the feeling and said she never saw it coming. "I'm a little frightened by it, to be perfectly honest," she said. "The values that were so close, Texas values, were so close to Oklahoma values, and more of a Christian state. And I hope that's still the case there." Curtis from Guthrie said, "All I can do is pray for them, because … I felt like they were deceived and lied to about some of the things that their politicians were talking about, and they're going to find out that they were." Curtis added that Oklahoma could be next if people stay home and don't vote. Larry, a small business owner from Guthrie, interviewed down the street from the diner, described the changing politics as shocking and one that "freaked out" many. BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS "Turning blue (Texas) is probably really good for Oklahoma," Larry argued, adding that conservative Texans were now fleeing to Oklahoma. Peggy from Guthrie speculated the same political shift could happen in Oklahoma, but she hopes it does not. "I can see it happening here because we're a chain reaction," she said. "What happens in one state normally goes over to the next state. I believe it could happen." Bob from Guthrie was unbothered by Oklahoma potentially turning blue, saying, "I think it would be just fine." Larry described Oklahoma as "small but mighty" and "the last vestige of freedom." "I hope they fix what's going on in Texas," he said. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Arkansas Arkansas residents walking around downtown Hot Springs, Arkansas, were less afraid of their state turning blue, but shared concerns over Texas’ blue wave. "I think it's nuts," said Mason from Beebe, Arkansas. Calvin, also from Beebe, said, "That's crazy to me, to think that my home state of Texas went blue. I think my parents are gonna have a fit about that." Joel from Rogers said, "I’m really glad … it’s about time. I'm very glad to see that they had an overwhelming vote towards the Democrats to hold Trump accountable." Angela from Hot Springs said, "I think it's crazy to be honest. I never thought that would happen. I lived in Texas for 13 years, and I'm just really, I'm just shocked." Jana, who lives in Hot Springs, said, "We are from Texas originally and can't believe it. We are diehard conservatives all the way." Anne from Bella Vista said, "Too many California people moving over there, we think." And would Arkansas go blue? "Never," said Mason. "They would never do that and, honestly, if they do that, I probably would have to move, to be honest … going blue is just not the way to go," he said. Joel, although he acknowledges Arkansas is a red state, said the state needs to turn away from MAGA. Calvin disagreed with his friend and said it was just "a matter of time." "I think it's bound to happen at some point," he said. "I think each state is kind of following their own curve there." "I would hope not. We live in a conservative area of the state and I don't think that's going to happen," said Jana. Steve said, "I'm not sure it'll happen and hopefully it will not." Angela said Arkansas is staying red and called the state "stubborn" in that aspect. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES Louisiana Louisiana residents in Richland Parish can’t imagine their state turning blue and are concerned for Texans. Josh from Lafayette shared what would happen if his state turned blue. "I think, first of all, you'd see ammunition sales go through the roof," he said. Similar sentiment was shared among other residents who spoke to Fox News Digital. Robert from Oak Grove reacted to Texas electing Democrats, saying, "I think they're in a world of trouble." Calvin from Monroe, shared a different perspective, saying, "I think it's time for a change." However, Calvin added, "I don't vote across party lines but … I'm a Christian conservative, but I really don't have any opinion." Mark from Lafayette said, "I was kind of surprised to tell you the truth because I wouldn't have thought it would have happened that quickly." Mark said he is curious to see what happens in the next election before determining if Texas has been taken over by the left. Glen, a Richland Parish resident originally from Mississippi, said if it happened in Texas the possibility is there. "I could never see Texas going blue, so I guess I could," he said. Russell from Rayville said, "Oh, I hope not," adding that if Louisiana went blue, he would have to move "to another state." "Not anytime soon. I think the conservatives have got a good stronghold here," Mark said. Josh said he would be surprised to see the state turn blue. "That being said, I thought the same thing of Texas, so we'll see. I do think that the roots run deep here in Louisiana, and they're proud of it," he added. Calvin agreed that he doesn't see the state changing politically and something "drastic" would have to occur for this to happen. "I think it is hardcore conservative," he said. Robert had a similar take. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS AP "I think with the small communities that have, we're more connected to our land and our government. So, I think that we can hang on to red," he said.

articles.title: Illuminated Moon sculpture wows visitors in Jersey
articles.summary: People can see the 6m-wide sculpture in St Helier until 29 November.
articles.body:
People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.

ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.

The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.

Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."

The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir .

The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".

Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".

Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".

"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.

Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.

"We always just see little snapshots of it."

Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".

Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."

He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.

"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

A string of tech glitches continued, this time affecting Chase Bank and United Airlines. And the U.S. is stripped of its measles-free status by an international health agency. All three are seeking something different, said Han Lin, China managing director for the Asia Group. “Putin probably wants recognition that Russia remains indispensable. Xi wants acknowledgement that China belongs at the center of global diplomacy, and Trump gets a stage for personal deal making with other major nuclear powers,” Han said. Trump is also expected to have a bilateral meeting with Xi — but talks will be made complicated by the Nvidia scandal, which has raised security concerns among lawmakers and Trump administration officials amid the U.S. and China’s race for global AI dominance. At around 6:30 p.m. ET yesterday, Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally, hours after customers had reported trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds. But after unspooling the story of “Box Mike” — a homeless man who was fatally struck by a car in Arizona nearly three decades ago — I realized how little I understood about the extraordinary lengths genetic genealogists sometimes go to in service of their craft. articles.title: Mozambique’s opposition leader stands trial over deadly 2024 protests
articles.summary: Venancio Mondlane faces five charges, the most serious being instigating ‘terrorism’.
articles.body:
Mozambique’s opposition leader has arrived at the country’s Supreme Court to stand trial over his alleged role in deadly protests that followed 2024’s disputed election results .

Venancio Mondlane addressed reporters outside the court in Maputo on Tuesday. He faces five charges, the most serious of which is instigating “terrorism”. If found guilty, he could be jailed for up to 24 years.

“I arrive calm and confident in my legal team,” Mondlane said.

Months of antigovernment protests broke out in Mozambique in 2024 after Mondlane came second in national elections. President Daniel Chapo and his Frelimo party beat Mondlane, extending Frelimo’s time in power to more than 50 years. Mondlane disputes the results, and his allegations of harassment of the opposition have been echoed by rights groups, including Human Rights Watch.

Following the elections in 2024, the organisation said the vote had been marred by political killings, widespread irregularities, and restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. Frelimo denies any wrongdoing.

Amnesty International says more than 300 people were killed during protests against the election results. It accused authorities of waging a crackdown against demonstrators, with police allegedly using unlawful force, mass arbitrary arrests and suppression of information.

Mondlane has also been charged with inciting “terrorism”, advocacy of crime, public incitement to a crime, and incitement of civil disobedience.

Thousands of people gathered for protests in response to calls by Mondlane to organise against the results. While preparing to challenge the vote, Mondlane’s lawyer and aide were shot dead.

Before Tuesday’s trial, Mondlane accused the government of attempting to silence him during a livestream on Facebook.

“The message being sent is that you must remain silent. You must remain in captivity, in prison, in darkness,” he said.

“In truth, Venancio is being used as an example to an entire generation: A warning that nobody should dare to rise up against the regime, against an empire of kleptocracy, or against the system of oppression that we have lived under for 50 years.”

Mondlane denies all charges against him.

articles.title: Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’?
articles.summary: Trump says Washington doesn’t need a deal with Tehran, while Iran rejects ‘no war, no peace’. Is the war at an impasse?
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that Washington is in no hurry to end its war with Iran.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform late last week. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, which joins the Gulf to the open ocean.

In the same post, Trump told Vice President JD Vance to give his “complete and total attention” to what Trump described as “corruption and crime” in Democratic-run cities. Vance led the talks with Iran, which produced a short-lived truce in June.

But Trump has given mixed signals in recent days.

Earlier last week, he said the war was “militarily … effectively over”, though he added that he “would not hesitate” to resume strikes if diplomacy failed.

Trump’s mixed messaging came as his Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 midterm elections, which Vance blamed on the deeply unpopular US-Israel war on Iran and its economic fallout, in particular soaring fuel prices.

Here’s what we know about where this war may be heading now and what history tells us about where frozen wars end.

Observers say Trump’s mixed messages – and Vance’s comments criticising the war – indicate a disagreement within the party, with at least some members of the administration more comfortable with leaving the conflict unresolved.

That could mean leaving the US naval blockade of Iranian ports in place and sanctions against Iran ongoing – both red lines for Iran, which has consistently stated that it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or resume peace talks until these are lifted, among other demands.

On November 9, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had ordered officials to end the state of “neither war nor peace”.

Pezeshkian added that Iran was ready to negotiate but would not yield to coercion. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that “the ball is now in the American court” – to accept its terms for talks or continue the war.

The term has no strict legal definition. It generally describes a conflict in which large-scale fighting has stopped or sharply declined, but no peace agreement or political settlement has been reached. The issues which caused the war remain unresolved.

The front lines or the balance of control then harden into a de facto reality – in this case, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Iran targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz that it says have not been authorised to pass, or firing missiles at US assets in neighbouring countries.

Both sides keep their forces in place, often separated by a ceasefire line or a buffer zone. They may agree to an armistice or a series of truces without formally ending hostilities, such as the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad, Pakistan, in June, which fell apart within weeks.

The phrase “frozen war” became common in the 1990s and 2000s as a way to describe conflicts in the former Soviet Union. These included conflicts in Transnistria in Moldova , Abkhazia and South Ossetia in Georgia, and Nagorno-Karabakh .

A frozen conflict is not necessarily a peaceful one. Skirmishes, blockades, economic warfare and periodic flare-ups are common. The defining feature is that neither side can impose a decisive outcome, and neither is willing to make the concessions a lasting peace would require.

Could the US-Israel war on Iran become a ‘frozen war’?

The war began in February, when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Talks in Pakistan in April produced a memorandum of understanding in June which paused the fighting and briefly lifted the US blockade. The truce collapsed soon after – primarily over disagreements about control of the Strait of Hormuz – and Washington reimposed its naval blockade on July 14.

“Diplomatically, we are already there and have been since July, when the June memorandum fell apart,” said Muhanad Seloom, an assistant professor in critical security studies at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies. However, he added that the word “frozen” “flatters” a conflict with a US blockade, attacks on shipping around Hormuz running at more than one a day and strikes in both directions.

The US has carried out limited strikes, including on Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island . Iran has attacked tankers using what it calls unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz. According to trade intelligence firm Kpler, only five commodity vessels crossed the strait on November 7, and none crossed the following day, despite US claims to be escorting ships through.

“The war has changed form, from an air campaign to a siege,” Seloom told Al Jazeera, “and sieges end when the besieged side either breaks or breaks out”.

For Trump, a serious escalation carries heavy political risk right now.

In October, a Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey found that nearly 70 percent of Americans believed the war was not worth fighting. Polls have also consistently suggested deep opposition to sending troops to Iran.

Following the crushing defeat in the midterms, which resulted in the Republicans losing control of the US Congress to the Democratic Party, Vance wrote on X that anyone who believed the war was worth “losing the Senate for the next 6 years” should argue so openly.

“With support for the war at 31 percent and Congress just lost, a ground operation is close to unsellable,” Seloom said.

Yet ending the war on current terms is also unattractive for the US.

Lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports – a move designed to stop oil exports, further crippling Iran’s economy – and leaving the Strait of Hormuz under contested Iranian control would leave Trump with nothing to show for eight months of war. It would arguably be a worse position given that the strait was freely open to all shipping up until the war began.

According to reporting by The Associated Press news agency, Trump has conceded that walking away with Iran’s current government in place would amount to a “defeat”.

“Ironically, there is no military solution that does not involve a ground component,” said Tallha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute. Trump is reluctant to commit ground forces, and the public is “wary of another Iraq or Afghanistan”. As a result, Abdulrazaq said, “this conflict will drag on as neither side is willing to back down on their negotiating positions”.

Abdulrazaq said Trump wants a deal that goes far beyond the 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran negotiated under President Barack Obama, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Under that, Iran committed to restrictions on uranium enrichment and submitted to regular inspections.

But Trump withdrew the US from the JCPOA during his first term. “He simply has no political wiggle room to accept a deal similar to it, and the Iranians are in no mood to even give him those terms,” Abdulrazaq said.

That leaves Trump “stuck between a rock and a hard place”, he said. The US president must either try to win the war decisively or accept lesser terms. Otherwise, the conflict will “stay frozen with the odd bit of tit-for-tat retaliation from either side”.

Abdulrazaq added that any serious US-initiated escalation of the war would most likely come within the next two months – before the US Congress formally comes under Democratic control.

Until January, Republicans hold slim majorities in the outgoing Congress. That gives Trump “a narrow window of opportunity”, Abdulrazaq said, particularly with three US carrier strike groups likely to remain in the region through December.

Outside that window, Abdulrazaq said, the White House would prefer “no war, no peace”. In his view, Washington believes “correctly” that the US can absorb more economic pain than Iran.

But the Doha Institute’s Seloom warned that the siege in and around the Strait of Hormuz will hold only while it remains without too much cost. “American deaths, a Hormuz shock that lifts fuel prices again, or intelligence that Tehran is moving its 440kg of highly enriched uranium would each end it,” he said.

Iran is in its own bind. It has set seven conditions for a formal ceasefire, the reopening of the strait and a resumption of peace talks. These include lifting the US naval blockade, sanctions relief, the release of frozen funds and an end to hostilities on all fronts, including by Israel in Lebanon and hostilities against Iran’s allies in Yemen and Iraq. Ghalibaf has said while the Strait of Hormuz could also then be reopened, it will “never return” to its pre-war, toll-free status.

But the Iranian economy is under severe strain as a result of the naval blockade, decades of sanctions and a renewed economic push by the US against countries and entities trading with it since the war began.

Iran’s official statistics agency has reported that the economy shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March and June. The central bank put annual inflation at 83.8 percent in September, and the rial has repeatedly hit record lows.

“Tehran’s primary non-kinetic option is engaging in diplomacy through regional mediators like Qatar,” Abdulrazaq said. “But Iran isn’t willing to cut a deal on the US’s terms, so the economic pressure will create ever-increasing desperate circumstances for the regime to contend with.”

Iran is “attempting to weather the storm of US sanctions by deepening its reliance on Chinese oil purchases , but this is being hindered by the naval blockade”, he added.

“Tehran’s only good move is a deniable one, worked through security channels,” Seloom said. “The Qatari formula would put inspectors back into the bombed sites as the blockade comes off.”

“The alternative is the ‘Sadat option’, a limited war to force negotiations, which is how Egypt broke its own ‘no war, no peace’ stalemate in 1973,” he said. “Ghalibaf’s talk of ‘sustainable deterrence’ suggests some in Tehran are tempted.”

Abdulrazaq said, “The enemy always gets a vote … Iran may decide to unilaterally escalate to break the US naval blockade and sanctions by causing global economic pain by attacking the Gulf Arab energy producers of the region”, adding, “piling international and domestic political pressure on the Trump administration to back off and cut a deal favourable to Iran”.

What does history tell us about frozen wars?

Previous frozen conflicts suggest that such stalemates can last for decades.

One example is the Korean Peninsula. The Korean War ended with an armistice in July 1953, but no peace treaty followed. More than 70 years later, the two Koreas remain technically at war, divided by a heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone.

Eastern Ukraine is a more recent and less stable example. After Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, fighting broke out in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region between Ukrainian forces and Russian-backed separatists. The Minsk agreements brought ceasefires but no settlement. For nearly eight years, the front line barely moved, though shelling continued. That freeze ended in February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Nagorno-Karabakh shows how a frozen conflict can thaw when the balance of power shifts. A 1994 ceasefire between Armenia and Azerbaijan held for a quarter of a century. Then a stronger Azerbaijan reignited the war in 2020, and in 2023 it retook the disputed territory entirely.

Analysts, however, argue that territorial stalemates such as the Koreas and Russia-Ukraine are a poor fit for the US-Israel war on Iran.

Seloom said the closer parallel would be Iraq between 1991 and 2003 – “a regime that survived a war and then 12 years of embargo and periodic strikes, four of them without inspectors”.

Abdulrazaq points instead to Iran’s history: the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s, when each side tried to cripple the other’s oil exports. The resulting “Tanker War” was defined by attacks on shipping and missile strikes on energy facilities, a campaign of economic attrition.

How would a frozen war on Iran be different?

Most frozen conflicts revolve around disputed territory and a fixed line of contact. The US-Iran confrontation runs through international shipping lanes, sanctions regimes and energy markets.

Seloom said the Iraq comparison breaks down at Hormuz. “Saddam’s containment sat on Iraqi territory, while this one sits on a waterway that carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas before the war,” he said, referring to former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

That makes a stable freeze harder to sustain. Every tanker attack risks a wider escalation. A frozen war here could look less like the Koreas’ quiet Demilitarized Zone and more like Ukraine’s Donbas before 2022.

Abdulrazaq said the global economy cannot indefinitely absorb a frozen conflict over such a vital chokepoint, and diversifying trade routes takes time and money. Both sides, he said, are “on the clock” economically, in a way that South Korea and North Korea, as well as Ukraine and Russia, have never been.

Gulf states, shippers and energy importers are all exposed, which gives mediators such as Qatar and Pakistan a strong interest in breaking the deadlock. For now, both Washington and Tehran insist time is on their side. But history suggests that frozen conflicts often outlast the leaders who allowed them to freeze.

articles.summary: Odisha opens 24 new Eklavya Model Residential Schools across 7 districts, raising operational EMRS to 71; 1,440 tribal students to benefit.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: State govt has operationalised 24 new Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) across seven districts, taking the number of functional schools in the state to 71 and expanding access to residential education for tribal students in remote areas.While the schools opened a month back, the admissions were completed recently, the ST and SC development department announced on Tuesday.According to department reports, with this latest addition, the state now has 71 operational EMRS schools against the 111 sanctioned for it, which is the highest allocation among states in the country. Of these, 47 schools were functional before the latest expansion.The new schools are expected to benefit around 1,440 students, providing them access to residential facilities, modern learning infrastructure and opportunities for academic and overall development.Mayurbhanj accounts for the highest number of new schools, with eight at Raruan, Jashipur, Sukruli, Gopabandhunagar, Saraskana, Bisoi, Badampahad and Bijatola. Keonjhar has five at Saharapada, Harichandanpur, Banspal, Ghatagaon and Telkoi, while Nabarangpur has four at Kosagumuda, Umerkote, Dabugaon and Raighar.Three schools have been made functional in Sundargarh at Tangarpalli, Subdega and Bisra. Rayagada has two at Ramnaguda and Padmapur, while Koraput and Kandhamal have one each at Padua and Tumudibandha, respectively.At the national level, 533 EMRS are functional across 25 states and one Union Territory.The EMRS scheme aims to provide quality education to tribal students, particularly those from remote and underserved communities. articles.title: California bridge toll hikes could hit drivers' wallets and ripple out to consumers
articles.summary: California's Bay Area bridge tolls will climb to $9 for FasTrak users and $10 for mailed invoices starting Jan. 1, 2027, as seven state-owned bridges face rate hikes.
articles.body: Drivers in one of the biggest states in the nation are venting over a new round of bridge toll increases that could soon cost some drivers $10 per crossing — and have a spillover impact on millions of others who never even cross the bridges. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new rates will take effect on seven state-owned bridges in California's San Francisco Bay Area, according to an alert from Bay Area FasTrak. Drivers using a FasTrak toll tag will pay $9 for a standard two-axle vehicle, while those with a registered license plate account will pay $9.25. Drivers who receive an invoice in the mail will pay $10, the alert said. MAJOR US VACATION DESTINATION COULD GET MORE EXPENSIVE AS OFFICIALS EYE NEW FEES The changes will affect the San Francisco-Oakland Bay, Antioch, Benicia-Martinez, Carquinez, Dumbarton, Richmond-San Rafael and San Mateo-Hayward bridges. (The Golden Gate Bridge is not included.) The Bay Area Toll Authority (BATA) told Fox News Digital the increases are needed to maintain, repair and operate the bridges as they age. "State law requires the Bay Area Toll Authority — working in partnership with Caltrans [California's Department of Transportation] — to keep the state-owned toll bridges structurally sound and in good repair," BATA said in a statement. "These bridges range in age from 13 to 90 years old, and maintenance and rehab costs increase as the bridges age." The new rates are part of a plan approved by BATA in 2024 that calls for five annual toll increases through 2030. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The authority said the increases were spread out, rather than imposed as a one-time $2.50 hike to reduce the impact on commuters. Money from the increases will be used exclusively for bridge maintenance, repairs and operations, according to BATA. Widespread impact Even residents who never drive across the bridges could feel the effects, as commercial delivery trucks face higher multi-axle tolls under the rate hikes. Businesses may pass some of those added costs in the supply chain along to consumers — potentially resulting in higher prices at numerous local diners, grocery stores, shops and other venues. Even with the widespread impact, residents of New York and New Jersey note that some of their area's bridge crossings cost far more than do those in the San Francisco Bay Area. Crossing the George Washington Bridge from New Jersey to New York City, for example, comes with a $23.30 toll by mail (no EZ-Pass), according to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. That same price applies to the Goethals Bridge when coming from New Jersey. The tiered pricing system was delayed until 2027. The 2027 changes in California, meanwhile, will introduce different prices based on how drivers pay. FasTrak users will get the lowest rate because electronic toll payments cost less to process than license plate accounts or mailed invoices, according to Bay Area FasTrak. The tiered pricing system was delayed until 2027 to give drivers more time to sign up for FasTrak. Those using a FasTrak tag will save $1 per crossing compared with drivers who receive an invoice. For commuters who regularly use the bridges, the costs can quickly add up. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Starting in 2027, a driver paying the $9 FasTrak toll five times a week would spend $45 a week on bridge tolls alone. Some Bay Area drivers have taken to Reddit to voice their frustration over the rising costs. "I have no choice but to drive back and forth on the Carquinez bridge every day for work," one user wrote. "This on top of all of the taxes that we already pay is ridiculous." "Bridges need money for maintenance, and that money has to come from somewhere." Others said the cost has changed how often they cross the bridges. "I avoid driving across the bridge whenever possible," another user wrote. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The community as a whole want[s] to see prices go back down. We aren't greedy. Five dollars should be enough," another commenter added. Not everyone opposed the increases. "Bridges need money for maintenance, and that money has to come from somewhere," one commenter wrote, adding that people who use the bridges should help pay for their upkeep. Drivers can expect additional increases in the coming years. FasTrak rates for two-axle vehicles are scheduled to rise to $9.50 in 2028, $10 in 2029 and $10.50 in 2030. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Those paying by invoice will continue to pay more, with the rate scheduled to reach $11.50 per crossing in 2030. Fox News Digital reached out to Caltrans for additional comment.

articles.title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine says the attack took weeks to plan, while the Kremlin vows to rebuild the strategic bridge.
articles.body:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the attack, though he is yet to comment.

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The Security Service of Ukraine said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title: Thieves damage cable at Wilstead, near Bedford, says Openreach
articles.summary: People are urged to look out for suspicious activity, including vehicles that appear at odd times.
articles.body:
About a mile (1.6km) of communications cable has been damaged by thieves, a network operator said.

Police officers were called to reports of cable theft in Cotton End Road, in the village of Wilstead, near Bedford, at about 02:00 GMT on Thursday.

Openreach, which builds and maintains much of the UK's broadband and telephone network, said about a mile of cable had been affected and engineers were working to repair the damage.

Bedfordshire Police said patrols would be increased, but it urged people in remote areas to remain vigilant and report suspicious activity.

Thieves had also struck on Luton Road, near Toddington, the previous day .

In May Openreach and recycling firm EMR joined forces with Crimestoppers to highlight the impact of cable theft.

They said it caused "widespread disruption" and cost the UK public more than £4.3bn.

Det Insp Ben Searle said: "Cable theft causes significant disruption to residents, businesses and essential services, and we remain committed to identifying and targeting those responsible.

"We are continuing to work closely with utility providers and neighbouring forces to identify offending patterns, share intelligence and disrupt this criminal activity."

Police urged people to keep an eye out for vehicles in remote locations at unusual times and anyone acting suspiciously near infrastructure sites.

Residents and landowners were also asked to look out for unexplained vehicle tracks or the sound of digging or machinery.

articles.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
articles.summary: What can Robert Pattinson's past movie roles tell us about what he might be like as James Bond?
articles.body:
He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?

Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.

The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.

"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast .

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.

Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."

Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".

Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast .

"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire .

"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."

Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."

Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond

Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007

So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?

Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.

"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.

"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees : "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.

"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote .

"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".

Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.

"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.

However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.

Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.

"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.

"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."

Collider's Collier Jennings named The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.

"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.

"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.

"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.

"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."

Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.

It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen, not as a villain but equally not as a hero.

"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."

Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.

The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time .

"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."

Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

articles.title: Former MLB pitcher Scott Erickson was found negligent in a crash that killed two boys; after a $176 million verdict and $1.17 million punitive award against him, he is seeking a new damages trial
articles.summary: Former MLB pitcher Scott Erickson seeks a new trial on damages after a $176 million jury verdict in a wrongful death case linked to a 2020 crash that killed two young boys. Explore the details of the case and his legal argument against excessive damages.
articles.body: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Scott Erickson is asking a California judge to order a new trial on damages in a wrongful-death lawsuit stemming from a 2020 crash that killed two young brothers, arguing that the jury's $176 million award was excessive.Erickson, who was found negligent alongside socialite Rebecca Grossman in the deaths of Mark Iskander, 11, and Jacob Iskander, 8, is not challenging the jury's finding that he shared responsibility for the incident. Instead, his legal team wants the court to reconsider the financial penalties imposed on him, according to the Ventura County Star.The jury awarded the boys' family $176 million in compensatory damages for wrongful death and emotional distress. It later ordered Erickson to pay an additional $1.17 million in punitive damages, while Grossman was ordered to pay $21 million in punitive damages, AP reported.According to the Ventura County Star, Erickson's lawyers filed a motion in October seeking a new damages trial. They argued that the compensatory award was unprecedented and would leave their client financially ruined.Why Scott Erickson wants the damages verdict reconsideredIn the motion, Erickson's legal team acknowledged the jury's decision to hold him partly responsible for the boys' deaths but argued that the amount awarded was disproportionate.His lawyers described the case as one in which emotions could run high and accused the Iskander family's attorney of appealing to the jury's emotions during closing arguments. They argued that the court should intervene because the verdict was influenced by passion and prejudice.The former pitcher has also asked the judge to remove the punitive damages imposed against him. His lawyers maintain that the compensatory award alone would leave him unable to meet the additional financial penalty.The Iskander family's legal team has opposed the request. According to the Ventura County Star, attorney Andrew Owen argued that a substantial award does not, by itself, establish that jurors were influenced by prejudice or emotion.In a court filing, Owen said the verdict reflected the evidence presented during the trial, including the family's losses and the emotional trauma suffered by the boys' mother and younger brother, who were also at the scene.He described the jury's decision as measured, noting that it had considered the figures presented by both sides before reaching its verdict.What happened in the 2020 crash that killed the Iskander brothers?The collision took place on September 29, 2020, in Westlake Village, California. Mark and Jacob were crossing Triunfo Canyon Road with their mother, Nancy Iskander, and their younger brother when they were struck by a vehicle driven by Grossman.Erickson was driving a separate vehicle ahead of Grossman. The two had reportedly met earlier and were travelling towards Grossman's home to watch the presidential debate.During the civil trial, the Iskander family's lawyer alleged that both drivers had been drinking margaritas and were speeding towards the intersection. He said Grossman was travelling at 73 mph in a zone with a posted speed limit of 45 mph.Witnesses said Erickson's black SUV passed through the crosswalk without hitting the children. Nancy Iskander testified that she grabbed her youngest son and moved out of the path of Erickson's vehicle. Grossman's white SUV then struck Mark and Jacob.Erickson's lawyer, Jeff Braun, stressed during the proceedings that his client's vehicle did not make contact with the children. Grossman's defence attorney, meanwhile, denied that she was intoxicated and argued that she had been distracted after seeing the boys' mother move out of the way of Erickson's vehicle.Grossman was separately convicted in 2024 of second-degree murder, gross vehicular manslaughter and hit-and-run driving. She received a sentence of 15 years to life in prison, according to AP.The civil case brought by the Iskander family against both defendants went to trial earlier this year in Van Nuys. The jury found Grossman and Erickson negligent and awarded the family compensatory damages, followed by the additional punitive awards.A hearing on Erickson's request for a new damages trial is scheduled for later this month.You use AI every day.
